analysis:
F_u = x/(1-x) F_(1^k) holds with 0 mismatches for all unbordered u of length 3..9 up to length 200. T_011 is
longer than Fibonacci only for n in {1, 2, 4}; for n <= 2e6 the difference (Fibonacci - T_011) is -1 three times,
0 429 times and 1 1999568 times; block checks up to L = 90 find no violation. The predicted average gain
log_lambda(1/(lambda-1)) fails for k >= 3 (0.2282 measured vs 0.2875 for k = 3).
assumptions: all unbordered patterns of length 3..9, lengths L <= 200 (exact integers)
exhaustive comparison n <= 2e6 and block-wise comparison up to L = 90
counterexamples: Average gain of 0111 over 111 for n <= 2^40: 0.2282, predicted 0.2875.
falsification: Any count mismatch, any n >= 5 where T_011 is longer than Fibonacci, or more than L equal-length n in a block.

hypothesis: T-C11-A: for every unbordered u of length k+1, the codeword counts satisfy f_u(L) = sum_{l<L} f_(1^k)(l) (generating function x/(1-x) times that of T_(1^k)); hence cum_u/cum_(1^k) -> 1/(lambda_k - 1) and T_u is shorter than T_(1^k) by log_(lambda_k)(1/(lambda_k - 1)) bits on average (exactly 1 bit for k = 2). T-C11-B: for n >= 5, T_011 is never longer than the Fibonacci code and is exactly one bit shorter except for at most L values of n in each block of F_L integers.
methodology: Exact count identities; exact length comparison; average length gap over [1, 2^40] from breakpoints compared with the predicted constant.
question: Why do unbordered terminators beat 1^k at practical sizes although 1^k has the larger growth rate?
